_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. Before you romanize any name, check here. status per entry: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship, give the citation in note), 'provisional' (your romanization, not found in outside sources), 'decided' (a project style call). If you find a better attested form mid-book, change it here AND grep every built chapter for the old form, then rebuild. Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored. Add/rename sections freely (people, organizations, places, terms, ...).

周恩来.cast: Founder of the CCP's intelligence and security work; ran the Central Special Branch from Shanghai and later the united-front and intelligence work from Yan'an and Chongqing.
周恩来.note: 1898–1976. The CCP's premier diplomat and, throughout this book, the presiding figure of its hidden front.

毛泽东.cast: Chairman of the Chinese Soviet Republic and, from the Zunyi Conference on, the CCP's paramount leader; in this book, a master user of intelligence.

陈赓.cast: One of the “Three Heroes of Whampoa”; chief of the Special Branch's intelligence section, later a PLA general.

顾顺章.cast: The Special Branch's working head and master of “special operations”; his 1931 defection nearly destroyed the CCP underground.

康生.cast: Alias of Zhao Rong; took over the Special Branch in 1932. Later notorious for the Yan'an “Rescue Campaign” and Cultural Revolution persecutions.
康生.note: 1898–1975. Born Zhang Zongke; “Zhao Rong” was a working alias.

李克农.cast: Foremost of the “Three Heroes of Longtan”; later ran the Xi'an liaison work and rose to head CCP intelligence.

钱壮飞.cast: One of the “Three Heroes of Longtan”; confidential secretary to the Nationalist agent chief Xu Enzeng, whose warning saved the CCP Center in 1931.

胡底.cast: One of the “Three Heroes of Longtan”; ran the Nationalist intelligence organ in Tianjin from within.
胡底.note: 1905–1935. Killed on the Long March in Zhang Guotao's purge.

蒋介石.cast: Leader of the Nationalists (Kuomintang) and, in this book, the CCP's chief adversary on the hidden front.

戴笠.cast: Founding head of the Nationalist military secret service that became Juntong; Chiang Kai-shek's spymaster.

张学良.note: 1901–2001. The “Young Marshal,” commander of the Northeast Army; co-author of the 1936 Xi'an Incident.

中央特科.note: The CCP's first professional intelligence and security organ, founded by Zhou Enlai in Shanghai in November 1927; its four sections covered general affairs, intelligence, armed action (the “Red Squad”), and radio.

国家政治保卫局.note: The Chinese Soviet Republic's political-security organ (1931–1935), modeled closely on the Soviet GPU; renamed the Northwest Political Security Bureau after the Long March.

中统.note: The Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Central Organization Department, the KMT's civilian/party secret service; grew out of the 1928 Investigation Section under Chen Lifu.

军统.note: The Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Military Affairs Commission, the KMT's military secret service under Dai Li; grew out of the 1932 Special Services Department of the Blue Shirts.

特务.note: The word this chapter anatomizes. Originally a neutral term for “special-duty” military work, it became, in the mouths of both parties, the loaded word for the enemy's spies and secret police. Rendered by sense in this translation, and kept as tewu where the author discusses it as a word.

潘汉年.note: 1906–1977. A literary man turned master of CCP intelligence and united-front work; deputy head of the Social Affairs Department, working from Hong Kong and Shanghai. Wrongly imprisoned as an “inner traitor” in 1955; rehabilitated in 1982.

张国焘.note: 1897–1979. A founder of the CCP and commander of the Fourth Front Army; Mao Zedong’s chief rival on the Long March. Defected to the Nationalists in 1938; later emigrated and died in Canada.

胡宗南.note: 1896–1962. Chiang Kai-shek’s favored Whampoa protégé and senior commander in the northwest, the “King of the Northwest”; his forces blockaded the Border Region and took Yan’an in 1947.

周兴.note: 1905–1975. Head of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region Security Office (the “Border Security”) through the Yan’an years; later a deputy minister of public security.

徐恩曾.note: 1896–1985. Head of the Nationalist Zhongtong; a nephew-by-marriage of Chen Guofu and a member of the “CC Clique.” His memoir is quoted throughout this book.

陈立夫.note: 1900–2001. Nationalist party boss who, with his brother Chen Guofu, led the “CC Clique”; founding director of the bureaus that became Zhongtong and Juntong.

王明.note: 1904–1974. Leader of the Moscow-trained “28 Bolsheviks” and the CCP’s representative to the Comintern; a rival to Mao whose successive “Left” and “Right” lines the author disparages.

康世昌.note: A younger Yan'an-born cadre; deputy chief and, on the recapture of Yan'an, chief of the municipal public-security bureau.

中央社会部.note: The CCP’s central intelligence and security organ from February 1939, headed by Kang Sheng; known within the Party as 中社部 (Zhongshebu). The bland name “Social Affairs” was itself a cover.

陕甘宁边区保安处.note: The Border Region government’s combined public-security and procuratorial organ, known for short as 边保 (Bianbao, the “Border Security”); the executing arm of Communist security work in Yan’an, and outwardly the government face of the Northwest Bureau’s Social Affairs Department.

邓小平.note: 1904–1997. Here a mid-ranking political officer in Yan'an; after Mao Zedong's death, China's paramount leader and the architect of its “reform and opening.”

卓琳.note: 1916–2009. Born Pu Qiongying, daughter of a wealthy Yunnan ham merchant; Deng Xiaoping's wife from 1939 to the end of his life.

罗青长.note: 1918–2014. A young Yan'an-trained intelligence officer and “living file,” aide to Zhou Enlai; later minister of the Central Investigation Department.

汪东兴.note: 1916–2015. Rose from Mao Zedong's Yan'an bodyguard to head of the Central Guard Bureau; a CCP vice-chairman in the years just after Mao's death.

许建国.note: 1903–1965. Born Du Liqing; a veteran security officer, deputy head of the Border Security and later head of the Jin-Cha-Ji Social Affairs Department. Rendered “Du Liqing” where the book uses his original name.

谭政文.note: 1910–1961. A Long March security cadre, deputy head of the Border Region Security Office; later a senior procuratorial official.

赵苍璧.note: 1916–1993. A northern-Shaanxi local cadre who rose through investigation work; minister of public security of the People's Republic from 1977 to 1983.

李启明.note: An intellectual cadre from Shanxi and son-in-law of Li Kenong; the youngest deputy head of the Border Security, later governor of Shaanxi. One of the author's interviewees.

陈龙.note: 1910–1958. From the Northeast anti-Japanese forces; Mao Zedong's guard at the Chongqing negotiations and a pioneer of Communist counter-espionage.

凌云.note: 1917–2018. A Social Affairs Department trainee; the first Minister of State Security of the People's Republic.

贺龙.note: 1896–1969. A founder of the Red Army and later a marshal of the People's Republic; died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

林彪.note: 1907–1971. A leading Communist general and later marshal; named Mao Zedong's successor, he died fleeing China after an alleged coup attempt.

江青.note: 1914–1991. A Shanghai film actress and Mao Zedong's fourth wife; a leader of the Cultural Revolution and a member of the “Gang of Four.”

聂荣臻.note: 1899–1992. Commander of the Jin-Cha-Ji base area behind Japanese lines and later a marshal of the People's Republic.

李宗仁.note: 1890–1969. Guangxi militarist and Nationalist general, victor at Tai'erzhuang; briefly acting president of the Republic of China, he returned to the mainland in 1965.

董必武.note: 1886–1975. A founder of the CCP; deputy head of its wartime Southern Bureau in Chongqing, and later acting head of state of the People's Republic.

叶剑英.note: 1897–1986. A Communist general and later marshal; in charge of liaison for the Southern Bureau, and decades on a decisive figure in the arrest of the Gang of Four.

李德.note: Chinese name of Otto Braun (1900–1974), the German Comintern military adviser to the CCP and the only Westerner to make the Long March.

布鲁.note: A White-area underground veteran; reconnaissance chief of the Border Security and head of its first Qilipu training class.

王炎堂.note: Born Huang Jintang; entered the Social Affairs Department at fifteen and became an expert on the Nationalist secret services; later a deputy minister of the Central Investigation Department and one of the author's interviewees.

三青团.note: The Nationalists' youth organization, founded in 1938 and folded back into the Kuomintang in 1947.

整风.note: The Yan'an Rectification, launched in 1942: Mao Zedong's campaign of ideological remolding and cadre screening.

熊向晖.note: 1919–2005. The most celebrated of the Communists' deep-cover agents; secretary to Hu Zongnan for a decade and, later, a senior diplomat and deputy head of the Central Investigation Department.

沈安娜.note: 1915–2010. The “red stenographer” who took down the Nationalists' confidential meetings for fourteen years; her husband Hua Mingzhi was her partner in the work.

白崇禧.note: 1893–1966. Muslim general of the Guangxi clique, nicknamed “Little Zhuge” for his generalship; deputy chief of the Nationalist general staff and later defense minister.

傅作义.note: 1895–1974. Nationalist commander in North China; his 1949 surrender gave the Communists Beiping without a fight, and he served the People's Republic as water-resources minister.

阎锡山.note: 1883–1960. The “model governor” who ruled Shanxi as his own domain for decades, trimming his sails between the Nationalists, the Communists, and the Japanese.

卢绪章.note: 1911–1995. The Communist businessman who ran Guangda Huaxing as a Party front and money-maker; after 1949 a founder of the state foreign-trade system.

陈嘉庚.note: 1874–1961. The pre-eminent overseas-Chinese leader of the South Seas, a Singapore rubber magnate and philanthropist; his 1940 visit to Yan'an turned him toward the Communists. Rendered in the Hokkien form by which he is universally known in English.

王世英.note: 1905–1968. A Special Branch veteran who ran Communist intelligence and united-front work in the North; later a provincial governor, he died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

吴德峰.note: 1896–1976. A founder of the Party's courier and intelligence systems; ran the hidden Xi'an intelligence station under a family cover and later held senior legal posts.

宣侠父.note: 1899–1938. A Whampoa first-class graduate and secret Communist working the Xi'an united front; his 1938 assassination on Chiang Kai-shek's order is the subject of section 6.

蒋鼎文.note: 1895–1974. A senior Whampoa-clique general and head of the Xi'an field headquarters; he carried out Chiang Kai-shek's order to kill Xuan Xiafu.

卫立煌.note: 1897–1960. Nationalist First War Zone commander; won over enough to give the Eighth Route Army ammunition, he was later suspected of Communist sympathies and eventually returned to the mainland.

邓宝珊.note: 1894–1968. Nationalist general holding Yulin north of the Border Region; a friend of the Communists from Yan'an, he helped negotiate the peaceful surrender of Beiping.

赵寿山.note: 1894–1965. Commander of the Northwestern Army's 38th Army, secretly guided by Mao Zedong; he defected to the Communists and became governor of Qinghai and then Shaanxi.

高崇民.note: 1891–1971. A leading Northeastern patriot who founded the Northeast Salvation Association; a bridge between the Communists and the Northeastern and Northwestern armies before the Xi'an Incident.

广大华行.note: A Shanghai pharmaceutical trading firm founded in 1932 and run from 1937 as a secret Communist enterprise, funding and covering the Party's intelligence work in Nationalist territory.

华润公司.note: Founded in Hong Kong in 1948–49 out of the Party's trading firms; today one of China's largest state-owned conglomerates.

八办.note: Short for 八路军办事处. The open liaison offices the Communists were allowed to maintain in Nationalist cities during the wartime alliance; rendered “the Eighth Route office(s)” or, where the author uses the bare abbreviation, “the offices.”

皖南事变.note: The January 1941 Nationalist attack on the New Fourth Army headquarters in southern Anhui (literally “the Southern Anhui Incident”), which shattered the united front.

韩练成.note: 1908–1984. A Nationalist general who secretly served the Communists from within; later a PLA lieutenant general.

阎又文.note: 1914–1962. A deep-cover Communist at Fu Zuoyi's side who helped bring about the surrender of Beiping; his identity was kept secret until 1992, long after his death.
